summary:
Osmaniye province has no trans-specific ordinance, enforcement programme, local institution or documented incident in the sourced material. A trans visitor to Osmaniye stands under the national framework of Türkiye, which applies here without local modification.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Türkiye since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and legal gender change has been available since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classed under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly.

Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied bans. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images on social media that were incompatible with 'society's moral values' and could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise any expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible to obtain; they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. In 2026 the draft judicial package's LGBTI-discriminatory provisions were removed. A February 2026 press report described a proposed law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison; it was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill (the 12th judicial package).

In June 2025 the Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency (Ministry of Health) banned the prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 draft packages and the February 2026 proposal on 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' did not reach parliament, but their repeated appearance indicates sustained legislative appetite for criminalising LGBTI expression and gender non-conformity. The removal of the discriminatory provisions from the 2026 judicial package shows the outcome is contested rather than settled.

Pride bans since 2015 have been enforced with tear gas, water cannon and mass detention in Istanbul and other cities, so event attendance carries a documented risk of force and arrest regardless of province.
localsOnly:
Residents of Osmaniye live under the national framework with no local modification: no anti-discrimination protection on sexual orientation or gender identity, no recognition of same-sex marriage, and exposure to the military-service 'unfit report' regime for conscripts who declare homosexuality.

Legal gender change has been available nationally since 1988, but the June 2025 Ministry of Health ban on prescribing and supplying hormones for gender-affirming procedures to people under 21 restricts access for younger residents. The İzmir court's December 2025 dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association signals the legal risk facing local LGBTI organisations nationwide.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three 2025 draft packages or the February 2026 proposal on 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

No Osmaniye-specific policing practice, detention data or facility conditions were located; the province-level picture rests on the absence of local signal rather than on documented local tolerance.
